Chapter 5

Setting Direction

设定方向

You rarely walk into a team with too little to do. More often, you inherit the opposite: a wall of priorities, each louder than the last, all of them deemed “critical.”

你接手一个团队时，很少遇到“没事可做”的情况。更常见的是相反的情形：一堵优先级的墙，每一个都比上一个喊得更响，而且每一个都被标注为“关键”。

When Juan led Stripe’s LATAM engineering team, the outside story was all momentum. Headlines talked expansion: new markets, new products, new partnerships. Inside, the truth was rougher: a growing team facing 30 competing priorities, and no clear agreement on what mattered most.

当 Juan 领导 Stripe 的拉美（LATAM）工程团队时，对外讲的全是势头。头条都在谈扩张：新市场、新产品、新合作。但里面的真相要残酷得多：一个不断壮大的团队，面对着 30 个互相竞争的优先级，却对“到底什么最重要”没有共识。

Some priorities were tactical: supporting existing customers, fixing bugs, maintaining deployments. Others were strategic monsters: exploring expansion into three new countries, navigating deep regulatory compliance in Mexico and Brazil, launching new local payment methods like OXXO and Boleto, and supporting internal infrastructure and security efforts across the company. Each request came with urgency attached and each one appeared to be high priority. So, the team said yes to everything.

有些优先级是战术性的：服务现有客户、修 bug、维持部署。另一些则是战略级的巨兽：探索向三个新国家扩张、搞定墨西哥和巴西复杂的合规、上线 OXXO 和 Boleto 这类本地支付方式、以及支持全公司的内部基础设施与安全工作。每个请求都自带紧迫感，每个看起来都很高优先级。于是，团队对一切都说了“好”。

On paper, it looked like progress—closed tickets, shipped code, and calendars stuffed with meetings. But underneath, the wheels were spinning. Engineers were stretched thin across regulatory compliance, customer support, expansion research, and new feature development. There was wasted energy leaking in every direction and doubts arose about whether the work even mattered.

纸面上看起来像在进展——关了 ticket、发了代码、日历塞满了会。但底下，轮子是空转的。工程师被摊薄到了合规、客户支持、扩张调研和新功能开发四面八方。能量朝各个方向漏走，人们开始怀疑这些工作到底重不重要。

From the outside, chaos looks like momentum. From the inside, it feels like drift. Drift doesn’t just waste effort; it erodes ambition. And that erosion happens to individual contributors just as much as leaders. When senior engineers can’t tell which technical decisions will matter next quarter, they stop making bold architectural choices. When junior engineers don’t understand how their tickets connect to outcomes, they optimize for getting through code review instead of solving real problems.

从外面看，混乱像是势头；从里面看，它像漂移。漂移不只是浪费力气，它还侵蚀雄心。而这种侵蚀，发生在普通工程师身上和发生在领导身上一样多。当高级工程师说不准哪个技术决策在下季度会重要时，他们就不再做大胆的架构选择；当初级工程师不理解自己的 ticket 如何连回结果时，他们就把“通过 code review”当成优化目标，而不是去解决真实问题。

— 原书第 95 页 —

A team also doesn’t earn the right to expand just by hiring more people. It has to work well first. Adding headcount without focus can make chaotic environments even worse. In the Stripe LATAM team, the breakthrough didn’t come from a new process or hiring spree; it came from clarity. During a virtual leadership off-site in the height of the 2020 pandemic, the reality check was brutal: engineering leads, product managers, operations, and legal team put all 30 priorities on the table. Each topic was debated and trade-offs were made explicit. They identified which problems were existential, which could wait, and which were just distractions in disguise. The arguments were messy, but within 60 days, the noise gave way to focused execution: six priorities total, two per team.

一个团队也不会仅仅因为多招人就赢得扩张的权利。它必须先运转良好。没有焦点地加人头，只会让混乱环境更糟。在 Stripe 拉美团队，突破并非来自一个新流程或一轮扩招；它来自清晰。在 2020 年疫情最严重时的一次线上领导层 off-site 上，现实检验是残酷的：工程负责人、产品经理、运营和法务团队，把全部 30 个优先级都摆上桌面。每个议题都被辩论，取舍被摊到明面上。他们分清了哪些问题是生死攸关的、哪些可以等、哪些只是伪装成优先级的干扰。争论很混乱，但 60 天之内，噪音让位于聚焦的执行：总共六个优先级，每个团队两个。

That shift changed everything. Engineers finally had permission to say no. Meetings got shorter and focus sharpened. Work started compounding instead of scattering. For the first time, momentum on the inside matched the story on the outside.

那个转变改变了一切。工程师终于被允许说“不”。会议变短了，焦点变锐了。工作开始叠加，而不是四散。第一次，内部的势头和对外的故事对上了。

That’s what direction is—not a perfect prediction of the future, but a path that stops your team from drifting. Good direction offers a way to help people move together, creating a shield against the drift that slowly drains energy and corrodes trust.

这就是方向——它不是对未来的完美预测，而是一条让你的团队不再漂移的路。好的方向提供了一种让人们一起前行的方式，为你挡住那种慢慢抽干精力、腐蚀信任的漂移。

While you’ll never have all the answers, good direction means creating enough clarity to let people move with confidence and to give your team permission to stop second-guessing and hedging—and start choosing.

尽管你永远不会拥有所有答案，但好的方向意味着创造足够的清晰，让人们能带着信心前行，并允许你的团队停止反复猜疑和两头下注——开始做选择。

This chapter is about that work: why direction matters, how drift creeps in, and how to create clarity, especially when it’s absent. It focuses on the cost of indecision, the power of saying no, and the discipline of consistently communicating the vision until everyone understands it.

本章讲的就是这件事：方向为什么重要、漂移如何悄悄潜入、以及如何创造清晰——尤其是在它缺席的时候。它聚焦于犹豫不决的代价、说“不”的力量，以及那种“反复传达愿景直到人人都懂”的纪律。

Chaos doesn’t disappear when you add more people or write more processes. It ends when you set direction.

混乱不会因为你多加人、多写流程就消失。它在你设定方向时才结束。

What Causes Drift

是什么造成了漂移

Drift doesn’t start with bad intentions. It begins when someone decides to keep options open, when a leader hedges on a priority because they’re unsure. For example, drift can happen when the product team wants to test both approaches instead of choosing one, or when the engineering team splits the difference on an architectural bet so each moment feels reasonable. These approaches run the risk of becoming toxic.

漂移不是带着恶意开始的。它始于某个人决定“保留各种可能性”——当一个领导因为不确定而在某个优先级上两头下注时。比如：产品团队想同时试两条路而不选一条，漂移就可能发生；工程团队在一个架构赌注上和稀泥、让每一刻看起来都合理，漂移也可能发生。这些做法都有变得有毒的风险。

The first symptom to look out for is language. Phrases like, “Let’s align on this,” “We’ll circle back,” or “We’re still figuring out the details” all seem harmless. But they’re actually warnings. They mean that no one wants to own the decision, or the team does not agree. So the team moves forward, burning energy on work that might not matter.

第一个要警惕的症状是语言。诸如“咱们先对齐一下”“回头再碰”或“细节我们还在琢磨”之类的说法，看起来都无害，但其实是警报。它们意味着没人愿意为这个决策负责，或者团队并没有达成一致。于是团队继续往前，把精力耗在可能根本不重要的工作上。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April saw this play out at PixelCurl within her first month. StudioOps engineers shifted their focus from asking, “Why are we building this?” to “Which ticket unblocks me fastest?” A senior engineer told her bluntly, “I used to care about architecture, but now I just care about getting through code review so I can move to the next thing.” That wasn’t cynicism; it was simply adaptation to drift.

April 在入职第一个月就在 PixelCurl 看到了这一幕。StudioOps 的工程师把关注点从问“我们为什么要做这个？”，变成了问“哪个 ticket 能最快把我解锁？”一位高级工程师直截了当地对她说：“我以前还在乎架构，现在我只在乎赶紧过 code review，好赶紧奔下一个。”那不是愤世嫉俗，那只是对漂移的适应。

Drift picks up speed once trade-offs go “underground.” For example, the sales team might promise a feature to close a deal, an exec might drop a “quick idea” in Slack, or the legal team might escalate something compliance related. Each request makes sense in isolation. But no one asks what stops to make room for the new. Priorities pile up because saying no feels riskier than saying yes. Engineers sense it first. They stop asking, “Why does this matter?” and start asking, “Which fires do I need to put out today?” That shift, from building toward something to just surviving the week, is drift taking hold. By the time leadership notices, the damage is done.

一旦取舍转入“地下”，漂移就会加速。比如：销售为了成单可能许诺一个功能；某位高管可能在 Slack 里丢一个“小想法”；法务可能升级一个合规相关事项。每个请求单看都合理。但没有人问“要停掉什么来给新东西腾地方”。优先级越堆越高，因为说“不”感觉比说“好”更冒险。工程师最先察觉到这一点。他们不再问“这件事为什么重要？”，转而问“我今天得先灭哪几处火？”那种从“朝某个目标建设”滑向“只是熬过这一周”的转变，就是漂移扎下根来。等到领导层注意到时，损害已经造成。

The Drift Diagnostic

漂移诊断表

When teams drift, the symptoms are often visible long before the underlying problems become critical. The diagnostic tool shown in Table 5-1 helps leaders to identify drift patterns early, and it provides concrete interventions to restore focus and momentum. Use this when you sense your team is spinning but can’t pinpoint exactly why.

当团队漂移时，症状往往早在深层问题变得危急之前就已经可见。表 5-1 这个诊断工具，帮领导者及早识别漂移模式，并给出具体的干预手段来恢复焦点和势头。当你感觉团队在空转、却指不清到底为什么时，就用它。

The Silent Cost of Drift

漂移的隐性代价

Drift rarely announces itself. It doesn’t look like failure. Instead, it looks busy. Tickets are closing, demos are scheduled, roadmaps are shuffled forward, and standups are full of updates. On the surface, things seem to be happening. But underneath, urgency has replaced clarity. People are sprinting, and no one can explain why.

漂移很少大张旗鼓地宣布自己。它看起来不像失败；相反，它看起来很忙。ticket 在关、demo 排上了、路线图在往前挪、站会上满是进展。表面上，事情好像在发生。但底下，紧迫感已经取代了清晰。人们在冲刺，却没人能解释为什么。

That’s drift: when effort no longer compounds. You hear it first in a standup meeting. Someone says, “Let’s just get something out” without explaining why it matters. Another engineer mentions they’ll “clean it up later,” but you both know later never comes. A product manager says, “The product team is still figuring it out,” and no one pushes back because everyone’s tired of asking. These can be indicators of what people say once they’ve stopped believing that the work they do is tied to anything real.

这就是漂移：当努力不再叠加。你最先会在站会上听到它。有人说“咱们先发点什么出去吧”，却不解释它为什么重要。另一个工程师说他“以后再收拾”，但你们都知道“以后”永远不会来。产品经理说“产品团队还在琢磨呢”，没人反驳，因为大家都问累了。这些都可能是一个信号：当人们不再相信自己做的工作和任何真实之物有关时，他们就会这样说话。

At first, drift feels like background noise. But drift compounds. Every unclear trade-off doubles the work, every abandoned priority leaves damage, and every shifting goal erodes trust. By the time morale collapses, the damage is already baked in.

起初，漂移感觉像背景噪音。但漂移会叠加。每一个不清不楚的取舍都会让工作翻倍，每一个被放弃的优先级都会留下损害，每一次摇摆的目标都会侵蚀信任。等到士气崩塌时，损害早已铸成、无法挽回。

And the cost is brutal. Execution slows because no one knows the absolute priority. Trust erodes because decisions don’t stick. Engineers stop taking initiative because they can’t tell what matters. Product managers optimize for marketing instead of impact. Leaders run meetings full of “updates” that don’t add up to progress. Top performers—the ones you count on to steady the ship—burn out fastest.

代价是残酷的。执行变慢，因为没人知道绝对优先级；信任被侵蚀，因为决策不持久；工程师不再主动，因为他们说不清什么重要；产品经理为营销而优化，而不是为影响；领导开着一场场满是“进展”却加不成任何进展的会。而顶尖绩效者——那些你指望稳住船的人——反而 burnout 得最快。

Juan saw this in the Stripe LATAM team before the off-site leadership ever took notice. The team was stretched across expansion research for three new countries while trying to deliver compliance requirements in Mexico and Brazil. Engineers spent days on regulatory documentation that might not matter if expansion priorities shifted. Others built payment method integrations that stalled when partnership negotiations changed. Global customers needed regional support, but the team couldn’t predict which requests would become long-term commitments. Energy scattered across too many fronts, none getting the focus needed to finish well. It only takes a few cycles like that before even the most motivated people shut down.

早在 off-site 之前，Juan 就在 Stripe 拉美团队看到了这一点。团队一边要交付墨西哥和巴西的合规要求，一边又被摊到三个新国家的扩张调研上。工程师花好几天写监管文档——可一旦扩张优先级变了，这些文档可能毫无意义。另一些人做支付方式集成，却在合作谈判一变时停摆。全球客户需要区域支持，但团队预测不了哪些请求会变成长期承诺。能量散在太多条战线上，没有一条得到“好好收尾”所需的焦点。只要几个这样的循环，即便是最有干劲的人也会关机。

Engineers stopped pushing bold ideas and instead optimized for survival: “Why bother cleaning this up if they’ll change direction next week?” Designers stopped asking for the reasoning behind decisions and just shipped what would get approved.

工程师不再提大胆想法，转而优化生存：“反正他们下周就改方向了，我收拾这个干嘛？”设计师不再追问决策背后的理由，只是发出那些会被批准的东西。

— 原书第 98 页 —

Managers stopped coaching and started counting tickets, because tickets were the only thing that felt measurable. People didn’t quit all at once, but they quit piece by piece, until the culture hollowed out.

经理们不再辅导，开始数 ticket——因为 ticket 是唯一感觉可度量的东西。人们没有一次性辞职，而是一点点地“离职”，直到文化被掏空。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

At PixelCurl, April inherited the aftermath. Two senior engineers had left in the previous quarter. Their exits weren’t dramatic, but they just quietly accepted offers elsewhere. The junior engineers who remained had stopped asking questions in standups because “Nobody knows what we’re supposed to be doing anyway.” One designer told April in a one-on-one, “I used to propose ideas, but now I just wait to be told what to build.”

在 PixelCurl，April 接手的是残局。上一个季度走了两位高级工程师。他们的离开并不戏剧化，只是悄悄接受了别处的 offer。留下的初级工程师们在站会上不再提问，因为“反正没人知道我们该干什么。”一位设计师在一对一里对 April 说：“我以前还会提想法，现在我只是等着被告知该做什么。”

The real damage isn’t wasted time; it’s what happens to the people. From the outside, dashboards stay green, demos look polished, and executive updates are full of slides showing “progress.” Leaders confuse activity with momentum, so by the time they notice the problem, the team is already exhausted.

真正的损害不是浪费的时间，而是发生在人身上的事。从外面看，仪表盘一直是绿的，demo 看起来很精致，给高管的汇报满是展示“进展”的幻灯片。领导把活动和势头混为一谈，所以等他们注意到问题时，团队已经精疲力竭。

Teams don’t collapse from one catastrophic failure; they erode, developing feelings of burnout, cynicism, and misalignment. People don’t leave because of one bad sprint—they leave because months of unacknowledged and unresolved drift convinces them that their work doesn’t matter.

团队不是因为一次灾难性故障而崩塌的；他们是被慢慢侵蚀的，逐渐生出 burnout、愤世嫉俗和脱节感。人们不是因为一个糟糕的 sprint 而离开的——他们离开，是因为数月不被承认、也不被解决的漂移，让他们确信自己的工作无关紧要。

But here’s what gives us hope: the opposite is just as true. Even a little clarity can flip a team’s energy. Drift drains momentum invisibly, but direction restores it instantly.

但有一点让我们看到希望：反过来同样成立。哪怕一点点清晰，也能翻转一个团队的能量。漂移在不知不觉中抽干势头，而方向能在一瞬间把它恢复。

What Good Direction Looks Like

好的方向长什么样

Drift shows you what happens when direction is missing: teams burn energy without progress, motivation erodes, and even the strongest people check out. But the inverse is just as powerful. When direction is clear, the same team that looked exhausted can rediscover momentum.

漂移让你看到方向缺失时会发生什么：团队耗着精力却没有进展，动机被侵蚀，连最强的人也会下线。但反过来同样有力。当方向清晰时，那支看起来已经精疲力竭的同一支团队，可以重新找回势头。

If drift is motion without meaning, then direction is focus with momentum. It doesn’t make the work easy but it makes it make sense.

如果说漂移是“没有意义的动作”，那方向就是“带着势头的聚焦”。它不会让工作变容易，但它让工作变得有意义。

Stripe’s LATAM payments team had been stuck in the same cycle—too many priorities, endless context switching, and constant noise. Then leadership made the call: narrow their efforts to shipping OXXO in Mexico, and Boleto in Brazil. Once the LATAM team forced priorities into the open, the team’s posture changed almost overnight.

Stripe 拉美支付团队曾困在同一个循环里——优先级太多、无止境的上下文切换、持续的噪音。然后领导层做了决定：把努力收窄到在墨西哥上线 OXXO、在巴西上线 Boleto。一旦拉美团队把优先级逼到台面上，团队的姿态几乎一夜之间就变了。

Senior engineers could finally challenge ideas without sounding cynical. Before, every debate felt endless. After all, why sharpen work that might be dropped tomorrow? Afterward, pushback was welcomed because everyone knew which trade-offs mattered.

高级工程师终于可以挑战想法而不显得像在冷嘲热讽。以前，每一场辩论都像没有尽头——毕竟，为什么要打磨一件明天可能就被砍掉的工作？而在那之后，反驳是受欢迎的，因为人人都知道哪些取舍才重要。

— 原书第 99 页 —

Junior engineers felt safer because they weren’t coding tickets into a void anymore. They understood how their work connected to outcomes in Mexico and Brazil. That clarity gave them confidence, and confidence accelerated learning.

初级工程师感到更安全了，因为他们不再把 ticket 敲进虚空里。他们理解了自己的工作如何连回墨西哥和巴西的结果。那份清晰给了他们信心，而信心加速了学习。

Product managers stopped competing over priorities. Previously, priorities shifted so quickly that project managers jockeyed for attention, trying to get their features approved before priorities changed again. After, they were aligned with engineers on the same outcome. They could defend choices, say “no” without damaging credibility, and trust that decisions would stick.

产品经理不再为优先级互相竞争。以前，优先级变得太快，项目经理们只能抢注意力，赶在优先级再次变化之前把自己的功能批下来。在那之后，他们和工程师在同一个结果上对齐了。他们可以为选择辩护，可以说“不”而不损害公信力，并相信决策会被坚持下去。

Team leads felt relieved. They weren’t the bottleneck anymore; they no longer needed to referee every trade-off or escalate every disagreement. With context, the team members made smart calls themselves.

团队负责人松了一口气。他们不再是瓶颈；不再需要为每一次取舍当裁判、把每一个分歧都升级上去。有了上下文，团队成员自己就能做出明智的决定。

Direction changes not just execution, but how people act. You can hear it in the way they talk. Someone who used to say “We’ll just get something out” starts saying “If we add this scope, we’ll miss the Brazil deadline.” Status updates that used to be vague and apologetic are now tied to outcomes, such as “This release unlocks the top payment methods in Mexico.” The shift isn’t cosmetic; it’s people finally understanding what they’re building toward.

方向改变的不只是执行，还有人们的行为方式。你能从他们说话的方式里听出来。一个以前说“咱们先发点什么出去”的人，开始说“如果加这个范围，我们就会错过巴西的 deadline。”那些以前含糊、带着歉意的状态更新，现在连回了结果——比如“这次发布解锁了墨西哥排名前列的支付方式。”这个转变不是表面文章；它是人们终于明白了自己在朝什么而建。

Meetings changed, too. Before, meetings consisted of endless debates, circling without resolution. After, meetings held sharper discussions, where trade-offs were named out loud and decisions were made that actually stuck. Slack threads got shorter, context switching dropped, and the energy that was once spent negotiating priorities went back into building.

会议也变了。以前的会议是无止境的辩论、绕来绕去没有结论；在那之后，会议的讨论更锐利，取舍被大声说出来，做出的决策真的能坚持下去。Slack 串变短了，上下文切换少了，那些曾经花在谈判优先级上的能量，重新流回了建设本身。

The technical challenge was still high—compliance projects are always tricky—but morale flipped. People leaned in again, taking pride in progress. The same team, the same talent, was suddenly compounding instead of dissolving. That’s what good direction looks like—not perfection or certainty, but just enough clarity for people to move with confidence.

技术挑战依然很高——合规项目向来棘手——但士气翻转了。人们重新投入，为进展感到自豪。同一支团队、同一批人，突然从“溃散”变成了“叠加”。这就是好的方向长什么样——不是完美、不是确定，而是刚好足够的清晰，让人们能带着信心前行。

Clarity can feel like a constraint in the moment. But in reality, it’s freedom. Saying no to everything that doesn’t align gives people permission to move fast and finish. The Boleto scope decision turned endless ambiguity into a clear priority: basic payments first, enhancements later. By making the limits explicit, the team finally aligned on what would happen, rather than focusing on what wouldn’t.

清晰在当下可能感觉像一种约束。但实际上，它是自由。对一切不对齐的事说“不”，就是允许人们跑得快、并跑完。Boleto 的范围决定，把无尽的模糊变成了一个清晰的优先级：先做基础支付，增强以后再说。通过把边界摆明，团队终于对齐了“会发生什么”，而不是纠结“不会发生什么”。

Good direction doesn’t remove ambiguity or trade-offs, but it makes ambiguity manageable and trade-offs clearer. You don’t need everyone to agree with the decision; you just need them to commit once it’s made.

好的方向不会消除模糊或取舍，但它让模糊变得可管理、让取舍更清晰。你不需要每个人都同意这个决策；你只需要他们在决策做出后投入承诺。

When direction is sharp enough, you see a consistent transformation: senior team members make clearer decisions instead of revisiting them, junior team members grow faster because they feel safe to ask and learn, product managers defend priorities instead of competing for attention, leaders step back from refereeing every debate and, most importantly, teams compound progress instead of dispersing effort.

当方向足够锐利时，你会看到一种一致的转变：资深成员做出更清晰的决策、而不是反复回头重议；初级成员因为敢问、敢学而成长更快；产品经理为优先级辩护、而不是抢注意力；领导从“为每一场辩论当裁判”中退出来；而最重要的是——团队叠加进展，而不是四散力气。

— 原书第 100 页 —

Direction is what unlocks autonomy and makes teams stronger. But most organizations don’t get there on the first try. They stumble into the same traps again and again. If you learn to spot them early, you can correct course before drift takes over.

方向是解锁自主权、让团队更强的东西。但大多数组织不是第一次就做到的。它们会一次又一次跌进同样的陷阱。如果你学会及早认出它们，就能在漂移接管之前纠正航向。

Traps That Cause Drift

导致漂移的陷阱

Most teams don’t fail because they lack talent. They fail because they fall into predictable traps. Oftentimes, chaos merely magnifies the problems that were already existing.

大多数团队失败，不是因为缺人才。它们失败，是因为跌进了可预测的陷阱。很多时候，混乱只是把早已存在的问题放大了而已。

No Clear Inputs

没有清晰的输入

Sometimes there isn’t a real strategy at all. Or worse, there’s a 40-slide deck that says everything but commits to nothing. Teams sit in limbo, waiting for clarity that never comes.

有时候根本就没有真正的战略。或者更糟：有一份 40 页的幻灯片，什么都说了，却什么都没承诺。团队悬在中间，等那份永远不会来的清晰。

At Stripe LATAM, this showed up as competing signals from different stakeholders. Global customers needed regional payment support. Expansion research suggested opportunities in three new markets. Regulatory compliance demanded immediate attention in Mexico and Brazil. Each signal made sense in isolation, but together they caused major sticking points. Engineers guessed at priorities. Managers stalled, hoping leadership would clarify. Nobody wanted to make architectural decisions because the strategy kept shifting. For the team, it felt like running in place. For leadership, it felt like “keeping options open.” It was drift in disguise.

在 Stripe 拉美，这表现为来自不同利益相关方的互相冲突的信号。全球客户需要区域支付支持；扩张调研指出三个新市场的机会；监管合规要求立刻关注墨西哥和巴西。每个信号单看都合理，但合在一起就造成了巨大的卡点。工程师在猜优先级，经理们在拖延，指望领导层来澄清。没人愿意做架构决策，因为战略一直在变。对团队来说，那感觉像原地跑步；对领导层来说，那感觉像“保留各种可能性”。那其实是伪装起来的漂移。

To avoid this, don’t wait for perfect clarity from above. Set a local mission, even a temporary one: “Here’s what matters for the next six weeks.” That gives your team a compass, even if the bigger map is still being drawn.

要避免这一点，别等上面给你完美的清晰。自己设一个局部使命，哪怕是临时的：“未来六周，重要的是这件事。”这会给你的团队一个指南针——哪怕更大的地图还在画。

Too Many Inputs

输入太多

The opposite problem is just as cumbersome. For example, within the context of our LATAM scenario, we could have multiple stakeholders with competing priorities, or global customers promising big deals if regional payment methods ship fast. In addition, legal teams might be escalating compliance issues that could shut down markets, partnership teams could be pushing integration deadlines, and internal infrastructure teams might need LATAM support for security audits. The backlog becomes a landfill of competing urgencies.

相反的问题同样棘手。比如，在我们的拉美场景里，可能有多个利益相关方各有互相竞争的优先级，或者全球客户许诺：只要区域支付方式快点上线，就能拿下大单。此外，法务可能在升级一些足以关停市场的合规问题，合作团队在推集成 deadline，内部基础设施团队可能需要拉美的安全审计支持。待办列表变成了一个堆满互相冲突的紧急事项的垃圾场。

Stripe LATAM lived here early on—with no less than 30 priorities, all labeled “critical.” Engineers felt whiplash between regulatory work and feature development. Product managers played politics, trying to get their initiatives prioritized. Everyone tried to get their request to the top.

Stripe 拉美团队早期就住在这里——不下 30 个优先级，全被标注为“关键”。工程师在监管工作和功能开发之间被来回拉扯。产品经理玩起了政治，想让自己的项目被排到前面。人人都在把自己的请求往顶端推。

— 原书第 101 页 —

The fix wasn’t a process improvement like a new project management software. Resolution came when making trade-offs explicit during a virtual leadership off-site. Leaders wrote down everything the team had been asked to do, and then chose. They created dependency maps, “not doing” lists—whatever it took to show that every yes had a cost. That’s how 30 priorities became 6.

解法不是上一个新项目管理软件之类的流程改进。真正的解决，来自一次线上领导层 off-site 上把取舍摆明。领导们把团队被要求做的一切都写下来，然后做选择。他们画了依赖图、列了“不做”清单——用尽一切办法，让“每一个 yes 都有代价”可见。30 个优先级就是这样变成 6 个的。

Hesitant Leadership

犹豫的领导

Sometimes leaders see the chaos but won’t step in. They confuse flexibility with indecision, and so they wait for certainty. Meanwhile, the team drifts.

有时候领导看见了混乱，却不肯出手。他们把灵活和犹豫不决混为一谈，于是等待确定性。与此同时，团队在漂移。

Before the LATAM off-site, Juan watched leaders quietly acknowledge the chaos but hesitate to make hard calls about market expansion versus regulatory compliance. They chose to delay rather than risk blocking growth opportunities. But inaction is its own decision—and it’s usually worse. For engineers, it felt like abandonment. For leaders, it felt like keeping options open. But it was neither. Clarity doesn’t require certainty. Sometimes, you just have to make the call, explain the why, and own the outcome. Even if you adjust later, you’ve given your team clear direction.

在拉美 off-site 之前，Juan 看着领导们默默承认混乱，却在“市场扩张 vs. 监管合规”之间的艰难抉择上犹豫不决。他们选择拖延，而不是冒“挡住增长机会”的风险。但不作为本身就是一种决策——而且通常更糟。对工程师来说，那感觉像被抛弃；对领导来说，那感觉像“保留可能性”。但两者都不是。清晰并不需要确定性。有时候，你就是得拍板、解释为什么、并为结果负责。哪怕你之后调整了，你也已经给了团队清晰的方向。

Reactive Roadmaps and Consensus Traps

反应式路线图与共识陷阱

Two traps often travel together. The first trap is roadmaps that shift with every escalation. Teams stop building toward outcomes and just react to the loudest voice. Sales demands a partnership feature. Marketing wants community features. Leadership wants payments compliance fixed. Before the LATAM off-site, directors waited for executives to force choices instead of committing themselves. Different stakeholders pushed competing timelines without owning the trade-offs.

两个陷阱常常结伴而行。第一个陷阱是：路线图随着每一次升级请求而变。团队不再朝结果建设，只是对最大的嗓门做出反应。销售要一个合作功能，市场要社区功能，领导层要修复支付合规。在拉美 off-site 之前，总监们等着高管来强行做选择，而不是自己承诺。不同的利益相关方推互相冲突的时间线，却没人认领取舍。

The second trap is the opposite: the endless search for consensus. Leaders wait until everyone agrees before deciding. This results in meetings that drag and seemingly endless debates. Nothing moves.

第二个陷阱正好相反：无休止地寻找共识。领导等到人人都同意了才做决定。结果就是会议拖沓、辩论似乎没完没了。什么都动不了。

Stripe avoided both when it chose to focus on Mexico and Brazil. The decision wasn’t unanimous. Some leaders argued to keep expanding. But once the call was made, everyone committed, and that is what mattered—not agreement, but commitment. Debate until the decision, and then support it.

Stripe 在选择聚焦墨西哥和巴西时，避开了这两个陷阱。这个决定并不是全员一致；有些领导主张继续扩张。但一旦拍板，人人都承诺了——而这才是关键：不是同意，而是承诺。辩论可以一直进行到决策那一刻，之后就支持它。

The way out of reactive chaos isn’t more meetings; it’s anchoring to outcomes. Instead of chasing features, define goals (e.g., “Improve reliability by 50%” or “Onboard 1,000 merchants”). Then, measure every new request against those outcomes. Without an anchor, every wave knocks you off course.

走出反应式混乱的路，不是多开会，而是锚定结果。不要追逐功能，而是定义目标（比如“把可靠性提升 50%”或“接入 1,000 家商户”）。然后，用这些结果去衡量每一个新请求。没有锚，每一个浪都会把你打偏航向。

These traps are predictable once you know them. Spot them early, and you can course correct before drift takes over. But not every threat to direction shows up this obviously. Sometimes the danger is quieter: the team looks productive, roadmaps shuffle forward, updates sound positive, but the work does not advance the real goals.

这些陷阱一旦你认识它们，就是可预测的。及早认出，你就能在漂移接管之前纠正航向。但并非每一个对方向的威胁都这么明显。有时候危险更安静：团队看起来很有产出，路线图在往前挪，汇报听起来很正面，但工作并没有推进真正的目标。

— 原书第 102 页 —

That’s when leaders need to be the lighthouse.

那正是领导需要做灯塔的时候。

Be the Lighthouse

做一座灯塔

After the obvious traps—too many inputs, hesitant leadership, and reactive roadmaps—the hardest part is leading teams once drift is already happening. Once drift sets in, what teams need most is a fixed point: a clear reference they can align to when they’ve lost direction. That’s your role as a leader: to be the lighthouse they can steer toward.

越过那些显而易见的陷阱——输入太多、领导犹豫、反应式路线图——之后，最难的部分是：在漂移已经发生之后，如何领导团队。一旦漂移扎根，团队最需要的是一个固定点：一个清晰的参照，好让他们在迷失方向时能对齐。这就是你作为领导的角色：做一座他们可以朝之航行的灯塔。

Drift doesn’t announce itself with alarm bells. Calendars stay full. Tickets move. Updates sound positive. From the outside, it may look like momentum. But from the inside, people are guessing. An engineer suggests we “refine it next sprint” because they’re not sure what completion looks like. A project manager says, “We’ll know more once we ship,” which really means “I don’t know if this matters.” Someone invokes “this came from the top” to end the debate instead of clarifying it. Individually, none of this is catastrophic. But together, it means goals aren’t clear enough to guide decisions.

漂移不会摇着铃宣布自己。日历依然满着，ticket 在动，汇报听起来很正面。从外面看，可能像势头；但从里面看，人们在猜。一个工程师建议“下个 sprint 再打磨”，因为他们不确定“完成”长什么样。一个项目经理说“发了之后我们就知道更多了”，而它真正的意思是“我不知道这事重不重要。”有人搬出“这是上面来的”来结束辩论，而不是澄清它。单拎出来，这些都不致命；但合在一起，意味着目标清晰到了不足以指导决策的程度。

Drift appears in the backlog. Every idea, escalation, or quick win lands without context. Nothing is evaluated against a single outcome. The backlog stops being a prioritization tool and becomes a seemingly never-ending list of tasks that no one seems to get to.

漂移出现在待办列表里。每一个想法、升级请求、快速收益，都毫无上下文地落进来。没有任何东西被放到同一个结果下去衡量。待办列表不再是一个排优先级的工具，而变成一张似乎永远列不完、却永远没人做完的任务清单。

Drift also reshapes behavior. Engineers stop asking if the work will matter and settle for whether it will pass review. Product managers become translators of competing requests instead of stewards of trade-offs. Leaders avoid providing clarity because they can’t promise certainty. The team adapts to the drift rather than fighting it and correcting it.

漂移也重塑行为。工程师不再问工作重不重要，而是退而求其次地问它能不能过 review。产品经理变成了互相冲突请求的翻译机，而不是取舍的守护者。领导回避提供清晰，因为他们没法承诺确定性。团队适应了漂移，而不是去对抗它、纠正它。

The emotional toll is real. The way that drift works is that instead of sparking outrage, it slowly dulls energy. People stop proposing bold ideas because they aren’t confident that the work will have an impact. They limit their ambition to what can survive review, sprint by sprint. It feels safe, but progress is slow.

情绪上的代价是真实的。漂移的运作方式是：它不激起愤怒，而是慢慢磨钝能量。人们不再提大胆想法，因为他们不相信这份工作会有影响。他们把雄心限制在“能活着通过 review”的范围里，一个 sprint 接一个 sprint。这感觉安全，但进展缓慢。

The solution isn’t a grand strategy deck. It’s a clear outcome and a short horizon—a fixed point to navigate toward.

解法不是一份宏伟的战略 PPT。它是一个清晰的结果和一个短的时间跨度——一个可以朝之航行的固定点。

The Stripe LATAM breakthrough happened when leaders created clarity during that off-site and defended it through months of competing requests afterward. The team knew why their compliance work mattered, even when it was tedious. They understood how OXXO and Boleto connected to regional growth, even when the technical challenges were brutal.

Stripe 拉美的突破，发生在领导们那次 off-site 上创造出清晰、并在之后数月里抵御住各种竞争请求守住它的时候。团队知道他们的合规工作为什么重要——哪怕它枯燥。他们理解 OXXO 和 Boleto 如何连回区域增长——哪怕技术挑战残酷。

— 原书第 103 页 —

The Boleto payment method also circled for months under a pile of reasonable requests: advanced fraud detection, multiple bank integrations, enhanced user verification, and adoption analytics. Every feature made sense for the Brazilian market. Together, they delayed the launch indefinitely. The drift broke when the team decided to focus on core functionality first: basic Boleto payments that worked reliably. Enhanced features would come after adoption was proven. So, the scope shrank, energy rose, and Boleto launched. Enhanced features were shipped in subsequent releases based on actual usage data. Brazilian customers got value faster, and the team rediscovered momentum.

Boleto 这个支付方式也曾在一堆“合理请求”下盘旋了好几个月：高级反欺诈、多家银行集成、增强的用户验证、采用率分析。每个功能对巴西市场都说得通。但合在一起，它们让上线被无限期推迟。漂移被打破，是在团队决定先聚焦核心功能的时候：可靠运行的基础 Boleto 支付。增强功能等采用率被验证之后再说。于是，范围缩小了，能量上来了，Boleto 上线了。增强功能则基于真实使用数据，在后续版本里陆续发出。巴西客户更快地拿到了价值，团队也重新找回了势头。

In both the Stripe LATAM prioritization and the Boleto scope decision, clarity came from framing near-term outcomes and repeating them until they felt obvious. It wasn’t a perfect map, but a clear point on the horizon.

无论是 Stripe 拉美的优先级取舍，还是 Boleto 的范围决定，清晰都来自：框定近期结果，并反复重复，直到它们变得不言而喻。那不是一张完美的地图，而是地平线上一个清晰的点。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April did this at PixelCurl by picking one fixed goal: ship a stable rendering pipeline for their top five clients by the end of the quarter. Everything else—the mobile app, the infrastructure rewrite, the experimental features—waited. She repeated it in every standup, every planning meeting, and every hallway conversation. Engineers initially pushed back, asking about the other priorities, but she kept redirecting: “Does this help us ship the rendering pipeline? If not, it’s not in scope this quarter.” By week three, the team stopped asking. By week six, they were moving faster than they had in months.

April 在 PixelCurl 就是这么做的：她挑了一个固定目标——季度末为前五大客户交付一条稳定的渲染流水线。其他一切——移动 App、基础设施重写、实验性功能——都先等。她在每一次站会、每一次规划会、每一次走廊对话里都重复这句话。工程师起初反驳，问其他优先级怎么办，但她不断把话题拉回来：“这能帮我们交付渲染流水线吗？不能的话，这季度就不在范围内。”到第三周，团队不再问了。到第六周，他们的速度是几个月来最快的。

If you inherit a drifting team, start small:

如果你接手了一支正在漂移的团队，从小处开始：

  • Name one outcome for the next cycle in plain language. Avoid vanity metrics; pick a goal that guides your decisions.

    用大白话为下一个周期点出一个结果。避开虚荣指标；选一个能指导你决策的目标。

  • Write a not-doing list and make it visible. Update it whenever you say no.

    写一份“不做清单”，并让它可见。每次说“不”就更新它。

  • Anchor status updates in one sentence: “We are doing X so that we can achieve Y.”

    用一句话锚定状态更新：“我们在做 X，为的是达成 Y。”

  • Create deadlines around uncertainty. If you can’t decide now, then set a date and define what will be true by then.

    围绕不确定性设 deadline。如果你现在定不了，就定一个日期，并定义到那时什么应当成真。

Drift doesn’t correct itself. You don’t wait for clarity to emerge. You create it by setting clear goals and repeating them consistently. Be the lighthouse.

漂移不会自己纠正。你不要等清晰自己冒出来。你通过设定清晰目标、并始终如一地重复它，来亲手创造清晰。做那座灯塔。

Creating Alignment

创造对齐

Setting direction inside a team is one thing. Making it stick across teams, functions, and leadership levels is another. Alignment is where most strategies fall apart—not because people are lazy, but because smart people optimize locally without understanding the broader context.

在一个团队内部设定方向是一回事；让它跨团队、跨职能、跨领导层级地坚持下去，是另一回事。大多数战略正是在“对齐”这里散架的——不是因为人们懒，而是因为聪明人在不理解更大上下文的情况下，做局部最优。

— 原书第 104 页 —

Why Alignment Breaks

对齐为什么会破裂

Misalignment rarely looks like sabotage. It often appears as if everyone is doing their job. Product managers chase customer satisfaction scores. Engineers chase technical elegance. Sales push revenue targets. Finance pushes margins. Each choice makes sense within that function’s frame of reference. But without a shared context, those choices cancel each other out.

不对齐很少看起来像蓄意破坏。它常常表现为：每个人都在做自己的本职工作。产品经理追客户满意度分，工程师追技术优雅，销售推收入目标，财务推利润率。每个选择在那个职能的参照系里都说得通。但没有共享上下文，这些选择就互相抵消。

Before the Stripe LATAM off-site, misalignment showed up more subtly. Different stakeholders optimized for their own metrics without seeing the bigger picture. For example, the partnerships team pushed integration timelines that conflicted with compliance requirements, and customer success promised features to close deals without checking engineering capacity.

在 Stripe 拉美 off-site 之前，不对齐表现得更隐蔽。不同利益相关方各自优化自己的指标，却看不见大图。比如：合作团队推的集成时间线，和合规要求相冲突；客户成功团队为了成单许诺功能，却不核对工程产能。

The cost of these individual decisions was measurable: new payment method launches were delayed by months, as teams worked on conflicting assumptions. Engineers couldn’t tell which regulatory requirements were firm deadlines versus aspirational goals. Customer features were half built because priorities shifted before anyone could finish the compliance work required to launch them.

这些个体决策的代价是可度量的：新支付方式的上线被推迟了好几个月，因为团队们在互相冲突的假设上干活。工程师说不清哪些监管要求是硬 deadline、哪些只是 aspirational（愿望式目标）。客户功能做了一半，因为优先级变了——在任何人来得及做完上线所需的合规工作之前。

Alignment Is Not Agreement

对齐不是同意

Alignment doesn’t mean consensus. It doesn’t mean everyone loves the decision. It means disagree and commit anyway: the decision stands, and everyone must commit their team’s full effort to making it work.

对齐不等于共识。它不等于人人都热爱这个决定。它的意思是：可以有异议，但依然投入承诺（disagree and commit）——决定已经定了，每个人都必须投入自己团队的全部努力去让它成。

At Stripe, the LATAM team faced a brutal trade-off: stabilize Mexico and Brazil first, or push expansion into three new countries. Everyone wanted growth. No one wanted to pause. Expansion was exciting, but stabilization felt like grinding compliance work. The debates were heated. But once the trade-off was named and the call was made, the team committed. Stabilize first, and then expand later. That choice gave the team clarity and the business real leverage in those markets.

在 Stripe，拉美团队面对一个残酷取舍：先稳住墨西哥和巴西，还是强推向三个新国家扩张。人人都想要增长，没人想暂停。扩张令人兴奋，而稳定感觉像枯燥的合规苦役。争论很激烈。但一旦取舍被说破、拍板完成，团队就承诺了：先稳定，后扩张。这个选择给了团队清晰，也给了业务在那些市场里真正的筹码。

Conflict in the open is healthy. Silence after the decision is dangerous. You want engineers to be able to say, “This timeline ignores regulatory testing; we will fail if we don’t adjust.” You want product managers to feel comfortable saying, “This request derails our focus and delays the Brazil launch by two weeks.” Expressing disagreement clearly will improve the work and surface real constraints. Pretending everyone agrees will slow progress and create problems later.

公开的冲突是健康的。决策之后的沉默才危险。你希望工程师能说：“这个时间线忽略了监管测试；不调整的话我们会失败。”你希望产品经理能坦然说：“这个请求带偏了我们的焦点，会让巴西上线推迟两周。”把异议清楚地表达出来，会改进工作、暴露真实约束。假装人人都同意，则会拖慢进展、并在以后制造问题。

— 原书第 105 页 —

How Leaders Create Alignment

领导者如何创造对齐

Alignment doesn’t happen by accident. Leaders make it happen through deliberate practices. Some of these practices are outlined here:

对齐不会偶然发生。领导者通过刻意的实践让它发生。下面列出其中一些：

  • Translate the mission into something concrete. “Expand across LATAM” is too abstract. “Enable the first 1,000 merchants in Brazil to accept payments” gives everyone a clear, measurable goal. Junior engineers understand how their work connects. Senior engineers know which technical decisions matter. The goal becomes tangible.

    把使命翻译成具体的东西。“拓展整个拉美”太抽象；“让巴西前 1,000 家商户能收款”则给了每个人一个清晰、可度量的目标。初级工程师理解了自己的工作如何相连，高级工程师知道哪些技术决策重要。目标变得可触可感。

  • Make the trade-offs visible. List everything openly. Use dependency maps, not-doing lists, or any tool that exposes hard choices. When the LATAM team listed all 30 priorities, the cost of saying yes to everything became impossible to ignore. The choice between breadth and depth was evident.

    让取舍可见。把一切都公开列出来。用依赖图、不做清单，或任何能暴露艰难选择的工具。当拉美团队把 30 个优先级全列出来时，“对一切都说 yes”的代价就再也无法忽视。广度与深度之间的选择，一目了然。

  • Close the loop after the debate. Encourage vigorous discussion until the decision point, and then conclude it: we have argued, weighed the options, and chosen—now we execute as one team. Run a commitment check. Ask each leader to state what the decision means for their team’s work. If the answers diverge, you’re not aligned yet.

    辩论之后把环合上。在决策点之前鼓励激烈讨论，然后收口：我们已经争论过、权衡过、也选择了——现在我们作为一支团队执行。做一次承诺检查。请每位领导说出这个决定对自己团队的工作意味着什么。如果答案分叉，你们还没对齐。

  • Shut down hallway politics immediately. The fastest way to slow progress is letting side conversations rewrite decisions made in the meeting. When someone starts undermining a call in private, address it directly: “We made this call together. If you have new information that changes it, let’s discuss it with the whole team. Otherwise, I need your full commitment.”

    立刻掐灭走廊政治。拖慢进展最快的方式，就是让私下对话改写会上做出的决定。当有人开始在私下里破坏某个决定时，直接处理：“这个决定是我们一起做的。如果你有改变它的新信息，我们和整个团队一起讨论。否则，我需要你全身心投入承诺。”

  • Show the impact of misalignment. Help people see the effect on customers when features are delivered incomplete. Show the cost to the team when senior people quit because they can’t tell what matters. Make local optimization costly by revealing its impact across the organization.

    展示不对齐的影响。帮人们看见：功能没做完就交付，对客户意味着什么。帮他们看见：资深的人因为说不清什么重要而离职，对团队意味着什么。通过揭示局部优化在整个组织里的影响，让它付出代价。

Alignment isn’t overhead. It’s the foundation that lets teams move fast without falling apart. It ensures that conflict improves decisions instead of dividing the team, that trade-offs stick instead of drifting, and that progress compounds instead of scattering.

对齐不是 overhead。它是那个让团队跑得快又不解体的地基。它确保冲突改进决策、而不是撕裂团队；确保取舍被坚持、而不是漂移；确保进展叠加、而不是四散。

— 原书第 106 页 —

Exercise: The Alignment Check

练习：对齐检查

After any major decision, run a commitment round with your leadership team. Ask each person to answer one question out loud: “What did we decide, and what does it mean for my team’s work this quarter?”

在任何重大决策之后，和你的领导团队做一轮承诺。请每个人大声回答一个问题：“我们决定了什么？这对我团队这季度的工作意味着什么？”

Listen carefully. If the answers diverge, if people heard different things, or if their interpretations point in different directions, you’re not aligned and you shouldn’t move forward. Repeat the decision and its implications until the answers converge.

仔细听。如果答案分叉了、如果人们听到了不同的东西、或者他们的解读指向不同方向，那你们还没对齐，就不该往前。重复这个决定及其含义，直到答案收敛。

The goal isn’t consensus but commitment. Everyone should be able to explain the decision consistently, even if they personally would have chosen differently.

目标不是共识，而是承诺。每个人都应能一致地解释这个决定——哪怕他个人本会做出不同选择。

Adapting Without Losing the Plot

在不跑题的前提下调适

Even with clear direction, plans will change. Competitors move. Regulations shift overnight. What mattered last quarter may not matter now. Change itself isn’t the problem; the problem is unexplained change.

即便有清晰方向，计划也会变。对手在动，监管一夜之间转向，上季度重要的东西这季度可能不再重要。变化本身不是问题；问题是“没有解释的变化”。

Unexplained change hits everyone differently, but it always erodes trust. Engineers feel whiplash. Product managers feel like they just broke a promise to their team. And leaders? They often think silence is safer than admitting uncertainty. It never is. Unexplained change erodes trust faster than bad news delivered clearly.

没有解释的变化，对每个人的打击不同，但它总会侵蚀信任。工程师被晃得脖子疼，产品经理觉得自己刚刚对团队食言。而领导呢？他们常常以为沉默比承认不确定更安全。从来都不是。没有解释的变化，比清楚传达的坏消息更快地侵蚀信任。

At Stripe LATAM, the pressure to expand was intense. Leaders wanted to open three new countries immediately. On paper, it looked like unstoppable momentum. On the ground, the team was barely stable in Mexico and Brazil, and regulatory obligations in both markets were piling up faster than they could address them. Expanding further would have created a compliance crisis that could shut them down entirely.

在 Stripe 拉美，扩张的压力巨大。领导想立刻开三个新国家。纸面上看，像势不可挡的势头。但在地面上，团队在墨西哥和巴西刚刚稳住阵脚，两个市场的监管义务堆积的速度比他们处理得还快。再往扩张走，会制造一场足以让他们整体停摆的合规危机。

The hard call was to focus on stability in Mexico and Brazil before expanding elsewhere. The message was direct: the mission remained regional growth, but the path was compliance and adoption first, then expansion. New markets would wait until the foundation was solid.

艰难的决定是：先聚焦墨西哥和巴西的稳定，再向别处扩张。信息很直接：使命依然是区域增长，但路径是先合规、先做采用，再扩张。新市场要等地基夯实之后再来。

Not everyone agreed. Launches were exciting and generated good press. Stabilization involved tedious compliance work that no one would notice until a problem arose. Some leaders pushed to keep expansion on the agenda, arguing that competitors would gain ground. Others quietly admitted relief; they’d been worried about the technical debt and regulatory gaps but hadn’t wanted to be the one to slow things down.

并非人人都同意。上线令人兴奋，还能换来好新闻。稳定则是枯燥的合规活，不出问题没人会注意。有些领导主张把扩张留在议程上，理由是对手会趁虚而入。另一些人则悄悄松了口气；他们一直担心技术债和监管缺口，但不想做那个踩刹车的人。

— 原书第 107 页 —

But once the trade-offs were clearly stated and the business risk explained, the decision held. The plan changed, but the core mission stayed consistent: build the foundation that enables the team to succeed in the region.

但一旦取舍被清楚陈述、业务风险被解释清楚，决定就站住了。计划变了，但核心使命保持一致：把地基打好，让团队能在这个区域成功。

If the Plan Changes, the Story Stays Intact

计划可以变，故事不能断

Plans change naturally as you learn, but stories endure as your North Star. If people understand why the plan shifted and how it connects back to the mission, they can accept it and adapt their work accordingly. If they don’t understand the connection, the same shift looks like chaos or failure.

随着认知加深，计划自然会变；但故事会作为你的北极星留存。如果人们理解了计划为什么变、以及它如何连回使命，他们就能接受它、并相应调整自己的工作。如果他们不理解这种连接，同一次变化看起来就像混乱或失败。

Direction isn’t about eliminating change. It’s about creating a strong enough framework for the team to adjust without losing coherence. When the story—the mission—is clear and consistently communicated, people can handle plan adjustments. But if the story keeps changing, everything falls apart.

方向不是要消除变化。它是要创造一个足够强的框架，让团队能调整而不失连贯性。当故事——也就是使命——清晰且被反复传达时，人们扛得住计划调整。但如果故事一直在变，一切都会散架。

Adaptation proves that clarity isn’t a one-time achievement. It has to be renewed every time plans bend, priorities shift, or new information emerges. Clear direction ensures the team can continue working effectively through uncertainty.

调适证明了：清晰不是一次性的成就。每次计划弯曲、优先级转移、或新信息出现时，它都必须被重新更新。清晰的方向，确保团队能在不确定中继续有效地工作。

And that points to the deeper truth running through this entire chapter: clarity isn’t extra work; clarity is the work.

而这指向了贯穿本章的那个更深的真相：清晰不是额外的工作；清晰本身就是工作。

Clarity Is the Work

清晰，就是工作本身

Teams don’t burn out from hard work. They burn out from unclear work. Long nights and strict deadlines are manageable if people understand why the effort matters. What drains them is pouring energy into tasks that shift, change, or disappear without explanation.

团队不是因为辛苦工作而 burnout 的。他们是因为工作不清不楚而 burnout 的。如果人们理解这份努力为什么重要，长夜和紧 deadline 都扛得住。真正把他们抽干的，是把能量倒进那些没有解释就摇摆、变更、或消失的任务里。

Direction is the scaffolding of leadership. Without it, even the most talented teams drift—busy, exhausted, and unsure if their effort matters. With it, those same teams compound progress and build momentum that survives setbacks.

方向是领导力的脚手架。没有它，即便是最有才华的团队也会漂移——忙碌、疲惫、还不确定自己的努力重不重要。有了它，同一批团队会叠加进展，建起扛得住挫折的势头。

At Stripe LATAM, clarity meant putting 30 competing priorities on the table during that virtual leadership off-site, naming trade-offs out loud, and forcing leaders to choose. That single process unlocked autonomy and gave engineers permission to say no to distractions.

在 Stripe 拉美，清晰意味着在那次线上领导层 off-site 上把 30 个互相竞争的优先级摆上桌、把取舍大声说出来、并迫使领导们做选择。单单这一个流程，就解锁了自主权，并允许工程师对干扰说不。

For Boleto, clarity meant setting a scope boundary: core payment functionality first, and add enhanced features only after adoption was proven successful. That constraint turned a stuck project into a shipped product. Features that had been debated endlessly suddenly had an answer—if it’s needed for basic payments, we build it; if it’s an enhancement, it waits for future versions. The clear scope enabled the team to execute effectively.

对 Boleto 来说，清晰意味着设定一条范围边界：先做核心支付功能，等采用被验证成功后再加增强功能。那条约束，把一个卡住的项目变成了一个上线的产品。那些被无休止争论的功能，突然有了答案——基础支付需要的，我们做；属于增强的，等以后版本。清晰的范围让团队得以高效执行。

— 原书第 108 页 —

Clarity also lives in team habits:

清晰也活在团队的习惯里：

  • No ticket, no work. Tasks not in the tracker aren’t considered active work. That single rule filters out noise before it reaches engineers.

    没有 ticket，就没有工作。追踪器里没有的任务，不算进行中的工作。单单这一条规则，就在噪音到达工程师之前把它滤掉。

  • The purpose of this meeting. Start every call by stating why it exists. If there is no purpose, then there should be no meeting.

    这场会的目的。每次开会先说清楚它为什么存在。如果没有目的，那就不该有这场会。

  • Asking anything. Keep an open channel where questions can be asked without fear and where doubts can be addressed.

    什么都能问。保持一个开放渠道，让人们可以毫无恐惧地提问、疑虑可以被回应。

None of these practices is glamorous. They won’t get you headlines or praise from executives. They may feel tedious. That’s the point. Clarity isn’t a heroic moment; it’s the discipline of repetition.

这些做法没有一个是光鲜的。它们不会让你上头版，也不会赢得高管的夸奖。它们可能感觉枯燥。而这正是关键。清晰不是一个英雄时刻；它是重复的纪律。

Leaders often tire of saying the same thing. They assume the message has landed because they’ve said it once, but it rarely has. The truth is that when you are sick of repeating yourself, your team is only beginning to believe you. Repetition isn’t laziness; it’s leadership.

领导常常厌倦了说同一句话。他们以为自己说过一遍，信息就落地了，但其实很少如此。真相是：当你厌倦了重复自己时，你的团队才刚刚开始相信你。重复不是懒惰；它就是领导。

And clarity isn’t necessarily about certainty. You will never have perfect information or be able to see the whole map. Clarity is about giving people a sharp point to navigate toward, even in uncertainty.

而且，清晰并不必然等于确定。你永远不会拥有完美信息，也永远看不到整张地图。清晰的意思是：哪怕在不确定中，你也给人们一个锐利的点，让他们可以朝之航行。

In addition, complexity doesn’t disappear and conflict doesn’t stop. Uncertainty is still there, but now people can navigate through it instead of drowning in it. Conflict sharpens decisions instead of fracturing teams, and uncertainty stops being an excuse to delay. You need a clear point that people can aim for, rather than a perfect plan.

此外，复杂性不会消失，冲突也不会停止。不确定性依然在那里，但现在人们可以穿越它，而不是溺在里面。冲突让决策更锐利，而不是撕裂团队；不确定性也不再是拖延的借口。你需要的是一个人们可以瞄准的清晰点，而不是一份完美计划。

In chaos, clarity is the rarest and most valuable gift you can give. It turns drift into direction, exhaustion into energy, and noise into momentum. It won’t feel glamorous or revolutionary. But it is the work that makes every other kind of work possible.

在混乱中，清晰是你能给出的最稀有、也最珍贵的礼物。它把漂移变成方向，把耗竭变成能量，把噪音变成势头。它不会让人觉得光鲜或革命性。但它是那种让其他一切工作成为可能的工作。

So, we repeat: clarity isn’t extra work; clarity is the work.

所以，我们再说一遍：清晰不是额外的工作；清晰本身就是工作。

— 原书第 109 页 —

Exercise: The Clarity Workshop

练习：清晰工作坊

Block 75–90 minutes with your team. Make sure all phones are down and laptops are closed. Depending on your setup, use one wall, board, or shared doc. The goal is establishing a sense of alignment. Use the following structure to guide your workshop:

和你的团队留出 75–90 分钟。确保手机都放下、笔记本都合上。根据你的环境，用一面墙、一块白板或一份共享文档。目标是建立一种对齐感。用下面的结构来引导你的工作坊：

  1. Map reality (20 min): Start by naming what’s true right now: current projects, deadlines, urgent issues, and unspoken frustrations. Write it all down without spin. Focus on honesty, not presentation.

    描摹现实（20 分钟）：先说出此刻什么是真的：当前项目、deadline、紧急问题、以及没说出口的沮丧。不加工地全写下来。聚焦诚实，而不是呈现。

  2. Choose the sharp point (15 min): Identify one or two outcomes that matter most this cycle. How will you know if you succeed? Encourage debate until the outcomes are clear. If the team can’t agree, that’s valuable information; surface the disagreement and resolve it before moving forward.

    选那个锐利的点（15 分钟）：找出本周期最重要的一两个结果。你怎么知道自己成功了？鼓励辩论，直到结果清晰。如果团队达不成一致，那本身就是有价值的信息；把分歧摆出来，在继续之前解决它。

  3. Draw the not-doing line (15 min): Make a visible list of the tasks that you are explicitly cutting or deferring. Every yes has a cost. This step is where you protect the team’s energy.

    画出“不做”线（15 分钟）：列一张看得见的清单，写下你明确要砍掉或推迟的任务。每一个 yes 都有代价。这一步，就是你保护团队能量的地方。

  4. Craft the story (10 min): Write one sentence, simple enough for anyone to repeat: “We are doing X so we can achieve Y.” Say it out loud until everyone understands it clearly.

    打磨故事（10 分钟）：写一句话，简单到任何人都能复述：“我们在做 X，为的是达成 Y。”大声说出来，直到人人都清楚理解。

  5. Commit together (10–20 min): Go around the room. Each person states what the decision means for their work. If answers diverge, stop and clarify until everyone is aligned.

    共同承诺（10–20 分钟）：绕场一圈。每个人说出这个决定对自己的工作意味着什么。如果答案分叉，就停下来澄清，直到人人对齐。

The artifact doesn’t matter. What matters is the conversation and shared commitment, not the notes on the board.

产物是什么并不重要。重要的是对话和共享的承诺，而不是白板上的笔记。

Reflection

反思

Take a moment to consider the following reflection points:

花一点时间思考下面这些反思点：

  • Which piece of work is your team doing right now that is drift (motion without purpose)?

    你的团队现在正在做的工作里，哪一件是漂移（没有目的的动作）？

  • What is one outcome you could name that would remove that drift?

    你能点出哪一个结果，能消除那种漂移？

  • If you had to defend your not-doing list in front of an executive, would you have the conviction to maintain it?

    如果你必须在一位高管面前为你的“不做清单”辩护，你有底气坚持它吗？

Figure 5-1 illustrates the drift recovery cycle.

图 5-1 展示了漂移恢复循环。

Conclusion: Pulling It All Together

结语：把一切串起来

The hardest part of setting direction isn’t the decision itself. It’s maintaining it long enough for it to guide the team.

设定方向最难的部分，不是决定本身，而是把它维持足够久、久到它能真正引导团队。

At Stripe LATAM, after the team finally cut down priorities, the pressure to add more never stopped. Sales requested exceptions, executives pitched quick wins, and partners escalated urgent requests. Every week brought a new reason to say yes, to keep options open, or to hedge just a little.

在 Stripe 拉美，团队终于把优先级砍下来之后，“再加一点”的压力从未停止。销售要求破例，高管推销快速收益，合作方升级紧急请求。每周都带来一个新理由，让你说 yes、让你保留可能性、或让你稍微两头下注。

What saved the team wasn’t a better process or a stronger roadmap. It was the leaders who kept saying no—not once, but dozens of times, in standups, in planning meetings, in hallway conversations. The repetition felt boring but it was the only thing that worked.

救下团队的，不是更好的流程，也不是更强的路线图。是那些一直说不的领导——不是一次，而是几十次，在站会上、在规划会上、在走廊对话里。这种重复感觉无聊，但它是唯一管用的东西。

Most leadership advice treats direction like a light switch: flip it once and the room stays bright. But real teams are messier. Direction is something you set, then reset, then defend, and then explain again. If you think you’ve said it enough, you haven’t. When you’re tired of repeating yourself, your team is just starting to believe you.

大多数领导建议把方向当成电灯开关：拨一下，房间就一直亮着。但真实的团队要 messy 得多。方向是这样一种东西：你设定它、然后重置它、然后捍卫它、然后再解释一遍。如果你觉得自己已经说得够多了，那其实还不够。当你厌倦了重复自己时，你的团队才刚刚开始相信你。

— 原书第 111 页 —

The other thing no one tells you is that setting direction makes you a target. When you say no to one priority, you’re saying no to someone’s project, someone’s promise, someone’s bet on what matters. People don’t thank you for clarity. They may push back, work around you, and complain that you’re slowing them down. Some of them may be right, but most of them aren’t. Your job is to hold the line anyway.

还有一件事没人告诉你：设定方向会让你成为靶子。当你对某个优先级说不时，你就是在对某个人的项目、某个人的承诺、某个人对“什么重要”的下注说不。人们不会因为你的清晰而感谢你。他们可能反驳你、绕开你、抱怨你拖慢了他们。他们中有些人可能是对的，但大多数不是。你的工作是无论如何都守住这条线。

Because here’s what we’ve learned after years of observing teams drift and recover: the teams that survive chaos aren’t the smartest or the most well funded. They’re the ones where someone decided what mattered and refused to let it slip. They set a direction, made it visible, and defended it past the point of comfort.

因为多年观察团队漂移与恢复之后，我们学到的是：熬过混乱的团队，不是最聪明的、也不是融资最多的。它们是那些“有人定了什么重要、并拒绝让它溜走”的团队。它们设定了方向、让它可见、并把它捍卫到超出舒服区的程度。

Drift is the default state. Direction is the work you choose to do instead.

漂移是默认状态。方向，是你选择去做的那件替代它的工作。

If your team is drifting right now, start smaller than you think. Don’t use a strategy off-site, or a new OKR framework. Pick one outcome for the next six weeks and make it so clear that anyone on the team can repeat it. Write down what you’re not doing and put it somewhere everyone can see. When someone asks you to add more, point to the list and say no.

如果你的团队此刻正在漂移，那就从比你想的更小处开始。别上什么战略 off-site，也别上新的 OKR 框架。为未来六周挑一个结果，把它做得清晰到团队里任何人都能复述。写下你不做什么，放到人人都能看见的地方。当有人让你再加东西时，指着清单说不。

That’s it: one outcome, one not-doing list, and six weeks.

就这样：一个结果、一份不做清单、六周时间。

You don’t need permission to do this. You don’t need executive alignment or a perfect plan. You need the conviction to create clarity when no one else will, and the stubbornness to defend it when people push back. The rest follows from there.

做这件事，你不需要任何人的许可。你不需要高管对齐，也不需要完美计划。你需要的是：在没人愿意创造清晰时，亲手把它创造出来的信念；以及在人们反驳时，把它捍卫下去的固执。其余的，自会随之而来。

In Chapter 6, we’ll talk about how to prioritize your new direction.

在第 6 章，我们会谈谈如何为你新设定的方向排优先级。
